title: The hour the railways made
text: {{1}} the nineteenth century, most towns kept their own solar time, read from the local sun. The difference {{2}} London and Bristol, for instance, was about ten minutes, and nobody minded. Missed trains were another matter: they became {{3}} common that railway companies began setting every station clock to London time. {{4}} the network expanded, the pressure for one single standard grew irresistible, and standard time was imposed {{5}} timetable rather than by law until 1880, when Parliament finally made Greenwich Mean Time the legal standard {{6}} Britain. The system worked so well that it was extended to the seas and then to the skies, and Greenwich time, born of railway necessity, became an authority {{7}} reach now extends to every phone and stock exchange on the planet. The world still measures its hours {{8}} the meridian the railways chose.

gaps.hint: time word: ___ the nineteenth century, towns kept
gaps.explanation: 'Until' marks the end of the old arrangement.

gaps.hint: preposition: the difference ___ London and Bristol

gaps.explanation: 'So common that' — degree plus result clause.
'As' introduces the parallel growth: as it expanded.

gaps.hint: preposition: imposed ___ timetable rather than by law
gaps.explanation: 'By timetable' — the means of imposition takes 'by'.
The standard applied within the country: in Britain.

gaps.hint: relative: an authority ___ reach now extends
gaps.explanation: 'Whose' links the authority to its reach.

gaps.hint: preposition: measures its hours ___ the meridian
